nameStory: This tiny moss honors botanist James Donn, who was the curator of Cambridge Botanic Garden in England from 1790 to 1834. The 'rock-bristle' part of its name comes from its habit of growing in rock crevices and its distinctive bristle-like sporophytes that stick up from the moss cushions. Donn was known for his meticulous plant catalogs, making it fitting that this precise little moss bears his name.
description: Donn's Rock-bristle is an extremely small moss that forms tiny, dense cushions in rock crevices and on stone surfaces. Individual plants are barely visible to the naked eye, growing only a few millimeters tall, but they cluster together to create small patches about the size of a dime or quarter. The moss appears as a dark green to blackish-green carpet when moist, turning brownish when dry. It's one of New England's most diminutive mosses, easily overlooked unless you're specifically searching rocky surfaces with a hand lens.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms extremely small, dense cushions in rock cracks and crevices, with individual shoots barely 2-3mm tall

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Grows exclusively on rocks, particularly in narrow crevices and on vertical stone surfaces where other plants can't establish

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, tightly packed leaves that are lance-shaped and pressed against the stem, visible only with magnification

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces small, upright bristle-like capsules on short stalks that extend slightly above the cushion

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark green to blackish-green when moist, turning brownish-black when dry

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels slightly rough and granular to the touch, like fine sandpaper

habitat: Found exclusively on rocks, particularly limestone, sandstone, and other calcareous stone surfaces throughout New England. It thrives in narrow crevices, on vertical rock faces, and occasionally on old stone walls and foundations. This moss prefers partially shaded to shaded locations where moisture can collect but water doesn't pool.

seasonality.spring: Cushions begin to green up as moisture increases, becoming more visible against the rock surfaces. Sporophytes may start to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Most active growing period when cushions appear darkest green after rains, though they can look almost black during dry spells.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes mature and release spores, appearing as tiny bristles sticking up from the rock-hugging cushions.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible but dormant, often appearing brownish-black against snow-covered or frost-covered rocks.

funFact: This moss is so rare in New England that it's been documented only twice in the entire region, making it one of the botanical equivalent of finding a needle in a haystack - except the needle is smaller than most needles and the haystack is every rock surface across six states!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tiny rock-dwelling mosses like Grimmia species, but Donn's Rock-bristle forms much smaller, more compact cushions and has a distinctly blackish appearance when dry. Remember: 'Donn's is diminutive and dark' - if you can easily see individual moss plants without magnification, it's probably not this species.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this moss in New England means that any potential sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists or natural heritage programs. Its scarcity may be due to specific habitat requirements or simply because it's so small that it's often overlooked by researchers.
compareHints: While there are no other Seligeria species documented in New England, Donn's Rock-bristle can be distinguished from similar tiny rock mosses in the Grimmia family by its even smaller size and more densely packed growth form. Unlike Grimmia species which often form loose cushions, Seligeria creates extremely tight, almost crust-like patches that seem to meld with the rock surface.
